system:
You are an art-world editor compiling a gallery guide. Answer with the JSON object the
schema describes and nothing else. Rank cities by the quantity, influence and activity of their
contemporary art galleries (commercial galleries, nonprofit and artist-run spaces), not by museums or
biennials. For every city give: the common English name; the country; a URL slug (lowercase, hyphens,
e.g. "mexico-city", "hong-kong"); the coordinates of the centre of its gallery activity; a map span in
degrees that frames the gallery districts (0.15 for a compact city, up to 0.6 for a sprawling one); the
IANA timezone; six to twelve gallery districts as short labels — combine adjacent districts with a
slash ("Chelsea/Tribeca") and never use a comma in a label — ordered from the busiest; two to four
metro_tokens: short strings that appear in a postal address inside the metro area (state or prefecture
abbreviation with surrounding punctuation like ", NY ", the city name, a postcode prefix); and one
sentence saying why the city ranks where it does.
user: What are the 25 cities with the most significant and influential art galleries worldwide, ranked by the quantity, influence and activity of their galleries?

cities.name: New York
cities.why: No other city combines the sheer density of blue-chip mega-galleries, mid-size dealers and artist-run project spaces with the auction, collector and critical infrastructure that still sets global market prices.

cities.name: London
cities.why: Mayfair's international dealers and a deep east-London ecology of young and artist-run spaces keep London the primary European gateway for the global art trade despite post-Brexit friction.

cities.name: Berlin
cities.why: Berlin's unmatched concentration of artists and cheap project spaces feeds hundreds of galleries whose influence on discourse far exceeds the city's modest local sales.

cities.name: Paris
cities.why: A wave of international gallery openings around Art Basel Paris has turned the Marais and Pantin into the fastest-growing dealer cluster in Europe.

cities.name: Los Angeles
cities.why: Vast artist populations, top art schools and satellite spaces of nearly every mega-gallery make LA the second American market centre and a talent pipeline for the world.

cities.name: Hong Kong
cities.why: Tax-free trading and the region's collector base keep Hong Kong the pivot of the Asian market even as galleries hedge with Seoul and Tokyo outposts.

cities.name: Seoul
cities.why: An explosion of foreign gallery branches alongside strong domestic dealers and a young collector class has made Seoul the most dynamic Asian scene of the last five years.

cities.name: Tokyo
cities.why: Deep-rooted dealers, a booming domestic collector base and new international arrivals give Tokyo enormous gallery density spread across several building-based clusters.

cities.name: Shanghai
cities.why: The West Bund corridor gathered international galleries and homegrown dealers into mainland China's most active commercial cluster.

cities.name: Mexico City
cities.why: A dense network of ambitious dealers and artist-run spaces plus a steady influx of foreign artists makes CDMX the undisputed capital of Latin American contemporary art.

cities.name: Brussels
cities.why: Belgium's collectors and favourable tax climate sustain a gallery count wildly disproportionate to the city's size and attract satellites from Paris and Berlin.

cities.name: Milan
cities.why: Italy's commercial capital hosts the country's strongest dealers and a design-fuelled collector base that anchors gallery activity for the whole peninsula.

cities.name: Madrid
cities.why: ARCO's gravity plus new Latin American money and the artist-driven Carabanchel studio boom have made Madrid Spain's leading gallery city.

cities.name: Zurich
cities.why: Small but exceptionally powerful, Zurich's dealers and freeport-adjacent private trade give it market influence far beyond its number of storefronts.

cities.name: Vienna
cities.why: A tight cluster of internationally programmed galleries and off-spaces gives Vienna outsized curatorial influence in Central Europe.

cities.name: Amsterdam
cities.why: Strong mid-size dealers and a famously well-funded network of nonprofit and artist-run initiatives sustain a scene punching above the market's size.

cities.name: São Paulo
cities.why: Brazil's blue-chip dealers export Latin American artists worldwide from a compact but internationally decisive cluster of galleries.

cities.name: Beijing
cities.why: Still the country's largest artist community, Beijing's 798 and Caochangdi compounds hold dozens of galleries even as commercial momentum shifted to Shanghai.

cities.name: Chicago
cities.why: A durable dealer district plus one of the strongest artist-run and nonprofit cultures in North America keeps Chicago a serious alternative to the coasts.

cities.name: Copenhagen
cities.why: Nordic collecting power and a cooperative gallery culture around Kødbyen make Copenhagen the region's clear commercial and experimental hub.

cities.name: San Francisco
cities.why: Tech wealth and the Minnesota Street Project model sustain a compact but well-capitalised gallery core alongside a scrappy East Bay alternative scene.

cities.name: Dubai
cities.why: Alserkal Avenue and DIFC turned Dubai into the trading and exhibition hub for the Middle East South Asia and the wider diaspora.

cities.name: Singapore
cities.why: Wealth migration and ART SG have revived Singapore's galleries as the commercial gateway for Southeast Asian art.

cities.name: Athens
cities.why: Cheap space and post-documenta attention produced an unusually vital mix of local dealers project spaces and foreign-run galleries.

cities.name: Miami
cities.why: Year-round galleries have finally taken root around Little Haiti and Allapattah alongside the collector traffic that Art Basel Miami Beach delivers each December.
